title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
After the meeting, I left early for my café shift, hoping to outrun the question.
Instead, I found a boy at the edge of a pond trying to walk on water.
He stepped forward. Sank. Tried again.
Each attempt was slightly different. "Why are you doing that?" I asked.
He shrugged. "Just to see if I can."
I started explaining why it wouldn't work—pressure, motion, fluid dynamics. He listened, smiled, and stepped forward again.
This time, I didn't see failure. Because he was exploring uncertainty.
Later, back at the café, I poured cream into a cup of coffee and watched it spiral into a vortex. The swirl was structured without being controlled, shaped by countless interactions rather than simple rules. Just like biology isn’t clean. It isn’t predictable. It’s more like that coffee—layers interacting, patterns emerging, complexity you can’t reduce without losing what makes it real. And I had done the opposite. The model failed because I built it the same way I spent years organizing my life: filtering anomalies. I had built a model that worked by smoothening complexity and variability. I had mistaken control for understanding. That night, I went home and deleted the model.

title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
That same mind never stayed focused on one thing for long.
Hypersensitivity made the world difficult to ignore. Every observation became a question, every question a potential obsession.
At five, I sat on the kitchen floor surrounded by my mother's lotions, pantry flour, and half-empty shampoo bottles. The plastic measuring cups from old medicine bottles became my beakers, their translucent walls perfect for observing chemical reactions that existed only in my imagination. Sticky goops that clung stubbornly to hair, foul-smelling potions that earned me banishment from the bathroom, and one memorable attempt at "invisible ink" that permanently stained our wooden table.
I'd press leaves between glass plates to try to create makeshift microscopes. Spiderwebs became engineering marvels to replicate, their intricate geometry defying my clumsy fingers. I'd spend hours observing ants building highways, then rush inside to sketch their routes in a notebook already filled with half-baked diagrams of flying machines inspired by maple seeds. Worn encyclopedias became sacred texts, while my bedroom doubled as an animal ER for injured birds, mice, and dragonflies. Long before I understood the science, I was captivated by the patterns behind it.

source: A life told through signal and noise
title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
In fourth grade, I built an incubator from a carton, tin foil, water trays, and a 40-watt bulb. For twenty-one days, I woke up at 2 a.m. to rotate eggs while my parents assumed I was simply playing with them. When the first chick finally emerged, I learned a lesson that would stay with me: curiosity rewards patience.
Years later, I began noticing a different kind of failed experiment. Curious students abandoned projects because the tools felt inaccessible. Small laboratories with ambitious questions spent more time navigating complexity than exploring it. Everywhere I looked, I saw potential waiting for an opportunity to become reality.
Living with flickering lights and empty bookshelves, I created SugarCODE, a platform, turning messy datasets into digital tools that let students and small labs explore biology where I once could not. I remember staring at the Nucleate semi-finalist email—I was the youngest in the history. Months later, walking Yale's campus for my full-scholarship programs, awe hit me as SugarCODE managed to raise $51,000 in funding.

source: A life told through signal and noise
title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
SugarCODE taught me something unexpected. I originally wanted to build software that helped people do biology more easily. What actually fascinated me wasn't just the interface—it was the network hidden underneath.
Every feature eventually pointed toward the same obstacle. Researchers weren't limited only by computation. They were limited by disconnected systems, inaccessible datasets, duplicated experiments, and institutions that couldn't easily collaborate. I realized I wasn't actually interested in building another biology tool. I was becoming interested in designing the infrastructure that biology itself depends on.
BioNet AI, a biocomputational tool I created, grew naturally from that realization.
Growing up in Assam, I became aware that many families around me carried blood disorders that were rarely discussed outside our communities. It wasn't simply the disease that struck me—it was the absence of data surrounding it. Conditions that affect millions globally can become practically invisible if the populations carrying them are underrepresented in research.

source: A life told through signal and noise
title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
I kept wondering how many discoveries never happen because the right data never meets the right researcher. How many organs fail to reach the best recipient because two databases never communicate? How many rare mutations remain statistically insignificant simply because the people carrying them were never included in the first place?
That question has stayed with me longer than any algorithm.
I don't think about BioNet as a transplant project. I think about it as an information problem disguised as a medical one.
We have extraordinary science. We can sequence genomes in hours, edit DNA with CRISPR, build AI systems that recognize cancer, and engineer proteins that never existed before. Yet hospitals still struggle to answer surprisingly simple questions: Where is the right donor? Which laboratory has the biospecimen? Has someone already collected data that could prevent this experiment from being repeated?
The bottleneck is no longer biology alone. It is coordination. Medicine has become increasingly precise while its infrastructure remains fragmented. Every hospital, laboratory, and biobank becomes another island. BioNet is my attempt to ask a different question—not how to build another better model, but how to redesign the ecosystem those models depend on.

source: A life told through signal and noise
title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
If someone handed me $1,000 tomorrow, I wouldn't spend it trying to make BioNet look bigger than it is. I'd spend it making it more real.
I'd purchase cloud compute to train larger federated-learning simulations, access higher-quality biomedical datasets where licensing permits, build more realistic synthetic hospital networks, and validate my assumptions against existing transplant and biobank literature. I'd also use part of it to speak with clinicians, transplant surgeons, and hospital administrators—the people whose constraints rarely appear in research papers but determine whether any technical solution survives outside a notebook.
The goal isn't to build a startup overnight. The goal is to replace my assumptions with evidence.
I don't have a medical degree. I don't run a laboratory. Most days I'm still a student trying to learn faster than my ideas arrive.
But I have something that has consistently pushed every project forward: I am unusually comfortable living inside unanswered questions.
I spent years apologizing for how quickly my attention shifted before I realized it wasn't drifting—it was connecting. A typography book made me rethink how clinicians should read patient dashboards. A documentary about coral reefs became a lesson in resilient networks. An article on consumer psychology quietly changed how I designed research software. Reading philosophy left me questioning whether the "best" algorithm was actually the fairest one. Even walking through a grocery store, I catch myself wondering why supply chains can track a mango across continents while hospitals still struggle to locate compatible biospecimens. My thoughts rarely stay where they begin. They wander just long enough to return with an idea that didn't exist before.

source: A life told through signal and noise
title: A life told through signal and noise
text:
Those childhood experiments never produced Nobel-worthy discoveries. But they forged something more valuable - a mind where every failure is just a question waiting to be rephrased. The slimes never solidified, the homemade microscopes barely worked, and most of my potions deserved hazard labels. Yet in that kitchen-floor laboratory, surrounded by sticky failures and wild dreams, the most important reaction occurred - a child's curiosity catalyzing into lifelong wonder.
For years, I viewed my hypersensitivity and OCD as obstacles. One flooded me with details; the other demanded certainty. Yet those same traits taught me to notice what others overlooked—a hidden assumption, an unexpected pattern.
I still notice the buzz of fluorescent lights. The difference is that I no longer wish I noticed less. Every overlooked detail, unexpected pattern, and unanswered question is a reminder that there is still more to understand—and that is exactly what excites me.

title: Better questions
text:
I deleted the model at 2:17 a.m, not because it failed.
But because it told me exactly what I wanted to hear.
And for the first time, that felt like a problem.
Three weeks of work—gone with a single command. The dataset was clean,
the predictions accurate, the code elegant. By every metric I used to
trust, it was right. And still, something about it felt dishonest.
Two nights earlier, I had presented the model to a small online group of
students and researchers. Someone asked a simple question I couldn’t
answer: What assumptions did you make about the system? I responded with
biocomputational-technicalities—parameters, constraints, optimization
functions. But the question lingered, unresolved.
After the meeting ended, I stepped away to escape it.
I left earlier than I needed to for my cafe shift.
And that’s when I saw a boy at the edge of a pond, trying to walk on
water.
At first, I almost ignored it. It looked pointless—no structure, no
progress. Just failure repeating itself. But something made me slow
down.
He stepped forward. Sank. Paused. Tried again.

title: Better questions
text:
Each attempt was slightly different—angle, force, hesitation. Not
structured enough to be a method. Not random enough to be meaningless.
So I walked closer.
“Why are you doing that?” I asked.
He shrugged. “Just to see if I can.”
I almost corrected him. Almost explained that it wasn’t possible. But
instead, I found myself explaining something else.
About pressure. About how water pushes back but not enough to hold
weight. About how motion matters—how fast movement can create lift for a
moment, like skipping stones. About how fluids behave—sometimes smooth,
sometimes chaotic.
About how even scientists don’t fully understand turbulent flow—it’s
still one of the hardest problems in physics.
He didn’t fully get it.
But he smiled anyway. Tried again. Failed again.
And this time, I didn’t see failure.
Because he wasn’t trying to eliminate uncertainty.
He was exploring it. He sure was resilient!
I left for the café, but something in me had shifted.
Inside, everything returned to systems I understood—orders, timing,
repetition. Predictable inputs, predictable outputs.

title: Better questions
text:
Until I poured cream into a cup of coffee.
It spiraled.
White folding into brown, forming a vortex—a shape created when inward
pressure balances motion, pulling liquid into a curved path.
It was structured in a way that didn’t need control.
Just like biology isn’t clean.
It isn’t predictable.
It’s more like that coffee—layers interacting, patterns emerging,
complexity you can’t reduce without losing what makes it real. Fluid
systems, like the swirl in my cup, are driven by interactions, not
simplifications.
And I had done the opposite.
I had built something that worked by removing complexity.
I had mistaken control for understanding.
That night, I went home and deleted the model.
Then I started again.
Not with cleaner data.
With better questions.
Before that, I wouldn’t have noticed the gap.
Last year, I would have been proud—thrilled, even—to produce something
that worked. My approach to science was straightforward: define the
problem, apply the method, get the result. When the inconsistency
persisted, I did what I always did: tried to “fix” it.
But the more I forced the data into coherence, the less I understood it.

title: Better questions
text:
I failed to understand–what if variability wasn’t noise, but
information?
And somewhere in that process, something else unraveled too.
I had always believed becoming my “best self” meant narrowing—choosing
one thing, mastering it, becoming it. That doing many things meant doing
none well.
But nothing I loved worked that way.
A boy at a pond became a lesson in uncertainty.
A swirl in coffee became a lesson in systems.
A failed model became a lesson in honesty.
It wasn’t linear.
It wasn’t efficient.
But it was real.
So who am I, without labels?
Not the student with perfect outputs.
Not the builder of clean systems.
Just someone who notices when something feels too perfect.
Someone who pauses. Questions. Starts again.
Someone who would rather understand complexity than erase it.
Becoming my best self doesn’t look like mastery anymore.
It looks like staying open.
Like following connections across things that don’t “fit.”
Like caring about small, strange moments—because they reveal something
bigger.
And maybe that’s enough.
Because I don’t want a life that’s perfectly defined.

title: Better questions
text:
I want one that keeps expanding.“Jack of all trades, master of none”…
only sounds like a flaw if you’re trying to finish a story that was
never meant to end there.

title: 4. Abstract of Research Paper submitted in 7th grade for Science Conference, Delhi
text:
Using computational modeling in Python 3.12.4, I designed a recombinant oncolytic Adenovirus Type-5 (Ad5) engineered to maximize the limited 7.5 kb foreign gene insertion capacity. The model integrates cytokines, monoclonal antibodies, immune checkpoint inhibitors, co-stimulatory molecules, immunomodulators, and BiTEs to enhance anti-tumor activity while reducing the cost and complexity of current cancer immunotherapies. The virus is packaged in liposomal carriers to improve delivery efficiency and tumor targeting.
The construct focuses on lung and pancreatic cancers by incorporating monoclonal antibodies and BiTEs specific to overexpressed Epidermal Growth Factor Receptors (EGFR). Simulation results demonstrated strong oncolytic potential: for every 100 tumor cells exposed to a single viral particle, only 2 cells remained viable. The engineered genome prioritizes genetic stability, reduced immune suppression compared to existing oncolytic platforms, and minimal pathogenicity in normal cells. This computational prototype provides a framework for developing next-generation, cost-effective oncolytic virotherapies.

childhood—sharp, almost high-definition clips. A red pen rolling off my
desk and landing cap-first on the floor. The exact pattern of rain dots
on the bus window during monsoon. A stranger’s ringtone—three rising
notes—playing behind me in a grocery line. They made no sense when I
dreamed them. But when they happened later in real life, the memory
snapped into place instantly, like a scene I’d already watched once. I
didn’t believe I could “see the future.” If anything, the precision of
these moments unsettled me. Eventually, I began wondering: Could these
dreams reveal something real—just not in the supernatural way I’d always

title: Premonition Research
text:
imagined? So I began researching. Psychology, memory consolidation,
pattern recognition, dream anthropology. Somewhere in that rabbit hole,
I found the Centre for Organizational Dreaming and emailed Emily Cook,
the co-founder. I expected silence. Instead, she wrote back—warmly,
thoughtfully—and invited me to explore dreams as reflections of meaning,
culture, and attention. Her response didn’t just inspire me; it gave me
a place to contribute. I began keeping meticulous dream logs—not poetic
entries, but almost lab notes. The shade of light in a room. The exact
wording someone used. Objects on a table. Background noises. I didn’t
just record dreams; I dissected them. Then I expanded outward,
collecting dreams from friends and classmates, anonymising and
categorising them before sending my dataset to the Centre as part of
their archival work. As I compared dreams to real events, I wanted
everything to fit neatly into logic—but it didn’t. My dreams didn’t feel
like guesses or stitched-together impressions. They were exact. The way
the raindrops curved on the bus window. The rhythm of a ringtone. The

title: Premonition Research
text:
crooked staple on a purple exam paper. I wasn’t just recognizing
patterns; I was recognizing moments, as if my mind had bookmarked them
before they happened. When I tried to explain this, most people laughed,
and the rest just nodded politely. It’s difficult to defend something
you can’t fully explain. But the clarity of those scenes wouldn’t let me
ignore them. I had only two options: ignore it, or investigate it.
There’s actually a term for this—pre-cognitive dreaming, which Oxford
describes as dreaming about an event before it occurs, often in a way
that feels eerily similar when the real moment arrives. What started as
confusion evolved into a methodical inquiry into how the subconscious
organizes information. It pushed me toward scientific skepticism,
careful observation, and a fascination with how much the mind records
without asking for permission.
But I’ll admit: when a moment arrives exactly as I dreamed it, I wonder
if the world is briefly more enchanted than it lets on (maybe just a
little?) and if the mind knows more than it seems on the surface.

title: 4. Abstract of Research Paper submitted in 7th grade for Science Conference, Delhi
text:
Using computational modeling in Python 3.12.4, I designed a recombinant oncolytic Adenovirus Type-5 (Ad5) engineered to maximize the limited 7.5 kb foreign gene insertion capacity. The model integrates cytokines, monoclonal antibodies, immune checkpoint inhibitors, co-stimulatory molecules, immunomodulators, and BiTEs to enhance anti-tumor activity while reducing the cost and complexity of current cancer immunotherapies. The virus is packaged in liposomal carriers to improve delivery efficiency and tumor targeting.
The construct focuses on lung and pancreatic cancers by incorporating monoclonal antibodies and BiTEs specific to overexpressed Epidermal Growth Factor Receptors (EGFR). Simulation results demonstrated strong oncolytic potential: for every 100 tumor cells exposed to a single viral particle, only 2 cells remained viable. The engineered genome prioritizes genetic stability, reduced immune suppression compared to existing oncolytic platforms, and minimal pathogenicity in normal cells. This computational prototype provides a framework for developing next-generation, cost-effective oncolytic virotherapies.

title: The agar dress
text:

The first time I grew a dress out of agar, my mother thought I had finally lost it.
It was 2 a.m., my desk was covered in petri dishes, and I was trying to coax patterns out of bacterial colonies the way a painter might coax color from a brush. This wasn’t for a biology assignment or a competition—it was part of my favorite STEM experience: an interdisciplinary bioart exploration with my mentor, Karen Ingram. Before this, I thought STEM meant problem sets, formulas, and clean right answers. This experience taught me that science could also be poetic, strange, and alive.
With Karen, I didn’t just study systems—I built them. I created miniature ecosystems in sealed jars, watching moss, fungi, and microbes negotiate space, resources, and survival. I experimented with phytomusic, converting plant signals into sound, listening to what photosynthesis might “say” if it could speak. I treated biology not as a subject, but as a collaborator.

title: The agar dress
text:
What made this my favorite experience wasn’t just what I made—it was how I learned to think. Instead of asking, What’s the correct answer? I began asking, What if? What if art could be an experiment? What if data could be emotional? What if creativity was a form of scientific inquiry?
Karen never gave me rigid instructions. She gave me questions. She encouraged me to document my work with sketches, journals, videos, and reflections, not just graphs. I learned to observe patterns, design systems, fail gently, and try again. Slowly, I stopped being afraid of ambiguity. I started to enjoy it.
That shift changed everything. It shaped how I now approach synthetic biology, computational research, and even entrepreneurship. I no longer see disciplines as separate silos. I see networks—feedback loops, interactions, ecosystems of ideas.
My favorite STEM experience didn’t teach me more facts. It taught me how to wonder with structure. It showed me that science doesn’t have to be sterile to be serious. Sometimes, it grows on agar, hums like a plant, and fits inside a glass jar.

title: The agar dress
text:
And sometimes, it looks like a dress.
The kitchen floor was my first laboratory. At five years old, I'd sit cross-legged surrounded by an arsenal of stolen ingredients - my mother's lotions, flour smuggled from the pantry, half-empty shampoo bottles. The plastic measuring cups from old medicine bottles became my beakers, their translucent walls perfect for observing chemical reactions that existed only in my imagination.
I conducted experiments with the seriousness of a lab-coated professor. Freezing mixtures, heating them and combining anything viscous enough to potentially become my holy grail - no-glue slime. The failures were spectacular. Sticky goops that clung stubbornly to hair, foul-smelling potions that earned me banishment from the bathroom, and one memorable attempt at "invisible ink" that permanently stained our wooden table.
Nature was my second teacher. I'd press leaves between glass plates to try to  create makeshift microscopes, marveling at the fractal patterns in their veins. Spiderwebs became engineering marvels to replicate, their intricate geometry defying my clumsy fingers. I'd spend hours observing ants building highways, then rush inside to sketch their routes in a notebook already filled with half-baked diagrams of flying machines inspired by maple seeds.

title: The agar dress
text:
The encyclopedia set in our living room, its spines cracked from overuse, was my sacred text. I'd drag volumes twice my weight across the carpet, tracing diagrams of snowflakes and beehives with reverent fingers. The cross-section of a bird's wing kept me awake at night - such perfect aerodynamics! I didn't understand half the words, but the numbers and diagrams spoke a universal language of wonder.
My bedroom doubled as an animal ER. Fallen nestlings with gaping beaks, field mice with injured legs, even the occasional stunned dragonfly - all found temporary refuge in shoeboxes lined with stolen cotton balls. I learned anatomy through necessity, fashioning splints from toothpicks and feeding tubes from eyedroppers.
Then came the Great Incubator Experiment of fourth grade during lockdown. Inspired by a library book, I converted my closet into a hatchery - desk lamp for heat, baking pan for humidity, and a stolen thermometer for precision. For 21 days, I lived by the incubator's rhythm, turning eggs religiously even at 2 AM. Even my parents thought I was just playing with the eggs. But then, when the first chick pipped its shell, that tiny wet creature embodied every scientific principle I'd ever chased: curiosity rewarded, patience validated, the invisible made visible.

title: The agar dress
text:
Those childhood experiments never produced Nobel-worthy discoveries. But they forged something more valuable - a mind that sees the world as endlessly interrogative, where every failure is just a question waiting to be rephrased. The slimes never solidified, the homemade microscopes barely worked, and most of my potions deserved hazard labels. Yet in that kitchen-floor laboratory, surrounded by sticky failures and wild dreams, the most important reaction occurred - a child's curiosity catalyzing into lifelong wonder.
